title: Turn the job ad into a checklist
body: Highlight every skill and responsibility in the posting and write one example from your experience next to each. Gaps you find now are questions you can prepare for instead of being surprised by.

title: Build a bank of five stories
body: Prepare five short stories about a success, a failure, a conflict, a time you led and a time you learned fast. Most behavioral questions can be answered by adapting one of them.

title: Check the latest company news
body: The day before, search for recent news, product launches or funding about the company. Mentioning something current shows real interest and gives you a natural question to ask.

title: Look up your interviewers
body: If you know who will interview you, check their professional profiles to understand their role and background. It helps you tailor examples to what each person cares about.

title: Practice answers out loud
body: Rehearsing silently feels fluent, but speaking reveals where you ramble or get stuck. Say your key answers aloud a few times, ideally timing them to one or two minutes.

title: Pack your interview kit
body: Prepare printed copies of your CV, a notebook, a pen, your ID and the interviewer's contact details. Having everything ready the night before removes last-minute stress.

title: Plan your route with a buffer
body: Check the travel time at the same hour of day and add at least 20 minutes of buffer. Aim to arrive nearby early and walk in 5 to 10 minutes before the start.

title: Sketch a 30-60-90 day plan
body: Write a few bullet points on what you would learn, deliver and improve in your first three months. Even if nobody asks, it sharpens your answers about how you would add value.

title: Own the first 90 seconds
body: First impressions form quickly, so greet everyone warmly, smile and use their names. A calm, friendly start makes the rest of the conversation easier for both sides.

title: Pause before you answer
body: Taking two or three seconds to think looks confident, not slow. It helps you choose the best example and avoid filling the silence with filler words.

title: Put numbers in your answers
body: Whenever possible, quantify impact: time saved, revenue grown, errors reduced or customers served. Concrete figures make your stories credible and memorable.

title: Clarify unclear questions
body: If a question is vague, ask a short clarifying question or restate what you understood. Answering the right question is better than answering quickly.

title: Keep answers to about two minutes
body: Long answers lose attention and short ones feel thin. Aim for one to two minutes, then check in with something like: would you like more detail on that?

title: Take brief notes
body: Jotting down key points the interviewer mentions shows engagement. You can refer back to them in your questions and in your thank-you message.

title: Match the interviewer's style
body: Notice whether the interviewer is formal or relaxed, fast or thoughtful, and adjust your tone slightly. Matching their pace builds rapport without losing your own personality.

title: End with a clear close
body: Before leaving, briefly summarise why you fit the role and confirm your interest. Then ask about the next steps and the expected timeline.

title: Explaining a gap in your CV
body: Be brief and honest about the reason, whether it was caregiving, health, study or a job search. Then quickly move on to what you did to stay sharp and why you are ready now.

title: Why are you leaving your job?
body: Focus on what you are moving toward, such as growth, new challenges or a better fit, rather than what you are escaping. Never criticise your current or previous employer.

title: Tell me about a failure
body: Choose a real but recoverable mistake, own your part without excuses, and spend most of the answer on what you learned. Close with how you applied that lesson later.

title: You seem overqualified
body: Address the hidden concern, which is usually that you will get bored or leave quickly. Explain why this role fits your goals now and how your experience helps the team from day one.

title: When you don't know the answer
body: Don't bluff. Say what you do know, explain how you would find the rest, and if possible reason through the problem out loud so they can see how you think.

title: Are you interviewing elsewhere?
body: It's fine to say yes without naming companies or details. Emphasise that this role is a strong match and share any timeline constraints honestly.

title: Handling inappropriate questions
body: In many countries, questions about age, religion, marital status or family plans are not allowed. You can politely steer back to your qualifications, for example by saying nothing will affect your ability to do the job.

title: Where do you see yourself in five years?
body: Show ambition that fits the path this role can offer, such as deeper expertise or more responsibility. Avoid naming a completely different career or the interviewer's own job.

title: Test the platform in advance
body: Install the video app, update it and do a test call with a friend a day before. Check that your camera, microphone and screen sharing all work on the device you'll use.

title: Put the camera at eye level
body: Raise your laptop on books or a stand so the camera is level with your eyes. Look at the lens when making key points so it feels like eye contact to the interviewer.

title: Get lighting and audio right
body: Face a window or lamp so your face is evenly lit, and avoid bright light behind you. Wired earphones with a microphone usually sound clearer than laptop speakers.

title: Choose a calm background
body: Sit in front of a tidy, neutral background and remove distractions from the frame. Tell people at home when your interview is and silence notifications on every device.

title: Use notes wisely
body: A few keywords on a sticky note near the camera can help, but don't read full answers. Interviewers notice when your eyes keep moving across the screen.

title: Allow for audio delay
body: Wait a beat after the interviewer finishes before you speak to avoid talking over each other. If the connection drops, calmly rejoin and briefly summarise where you were.

title: Have a backup plan
body: Keep your phone charged and the interviewer's contact details handy in case your internet fails. A mobile hotspot ready to go can save the interview.

title: One-way video interviews
body: For recorded interviews without a live person, treat the camera as your audience and smile at the start. Use any practice questions to check framing, then answer with the same energy as a live call.

title: Write a debrief right away
body: Within an hour, note down the questions asked, your answers, names and anything you would improve. These notes help with follow-ups and your next interviews.

title: Personalise your thank-you note
body: Send a short thank-you email within 24 hours that mentions one specific topic you discussed. A personal detail makes it memorable instead of generic.

title: Follow up at the right time
body: If they gave a timeline, wait until it passes before following up. Otherwise, a polite check-in about a week later is reasonable.

title: Connect professionally
body: Consider sending a connection request with a short note to the people you met. Keep it professional and don't use it to ask about the decision.

title: Handle silence calmly
body: Hiring processes often take longer than planned for reasons that have nothing to do with you. After one or two polite follow-ups, keep your focus on other opportunities.

title: Ask for feedback after a rejection
body: Reply graciously and ask whether they can share one or two things you could improve. Not everyone will answer, but useful feedback is valuable, and a positive reply keeps the door open.

title: Compare offers on the full picture
body: Look beyond base salary to bonus, benefits, leave, flexibility, growth and commute. Writing them side by side in a table makes the right choice clearer.

title: Keep your pipeline active
body: Don't pause your job search while you wait for one company's decision. Continuing to apply keeps your options open and reduces the pressure on any single interview.
